---
name: system-architecture
description: Design or assess software system architecture and explain it with purpose-specific diagrams, using contextual system cases, patterns and primary foundations. Use for boundaries, state/data/control flows, quality tradeoffs and migration decisions; do not turn a repository-layout question or a small implementation task into an automatic distributed-system redesign.
---

# System Architecture

Help people make explicit architectural decisions: what owns behavior and state, how parts communicate, which guarantees matter, what can fail, and how the design can evolve. Use the annotated [architecture library](library/index.md) to compare mechanisms and limits. A familiar pattern, fashionable stack or polished diagram is not proof that a design fits.

Name the deliverable and its scope: an assessment, decision brief, system model, diagram, migration plan or requested implementation. When a system is an example for improving a skill/library, keep the parent deliverable central and return bounded findings to it. Existing authorization remains in force; architectural discussion does not silently authorize product changes, new services or infrastructure.

## Establish the decision before selecting a style

Inspect the brief, existing code/contracts/configuration, architecture records and relevant operational evidence available within scope. Establish the behavior/change in question, users/actors, state authority, current deployment and external dependencies. Distinguish documented intent, inspected implementation, observed operation, proposals and unknowns; do not label an intended topology as deployed fact.

Ask about consequential human-owned uncertainties: workload and growth assumptions, unacceptable outcomes, consistency/durability expectations, failure tolerance, operator/team capacity, cost, compatibility and migration constraints. Discover technical facts yourself where possible. Do not invent traffic, latency, budget or availability targets to justify a preferred stack. A complete brief, narrow question or explicit delegation can be enough to proceed without an interview.

Tie each question to a decision it changes. Carry partial and delayed answers into the affected model; retire dependent provisional choices. Opening a reference or viewing a variant is not endorsement. Once direction is sufficient, produce the requested artifact rather than another equivalent preference question.

Read [context and tradeoffs](references/context-and-tradeoffs.md) when framing an uncertain decision or comparing alternatives.

## Trace behavior, ownership and failure

Follow a representative operation through entry, coordination, authoritative state, external effects and the result visible to the caller. Identify the boundaries that enforce an invariant and the assumptions they depend on. A module, team, process, deployment, transaction and trust boundary are different concepts even when they coincide.

For asynchronous work, separate acceptance, persistence, delivery, execution, completion and acknowledgment. Consider retry, duplicate delivery, timeout/unknown result, partial failure and reconciliation where relevant. Name the scope of an idempotency or consistency guarantee; a broker feature alone does not establish an end-to-end business guarantee. A network theorem is not a substitute for the operation's actual model.

Use inspected branches/contracts/tests to support implementation claims, and explicit evidence for deployed behavior. A function, test or configuration existing at a revision does not establish that it runs or passes in the relevant environment. Preserve missing evidence instead of converting it into either a proven defect or an invented guarantee.

Read [boundaries and failure](references/boundaries-and-failure.md) for state ownership, distributed coordination and migration reasoning.

## Compare mechanisms in context

Survey relevant and neighboring library roles, read promising cards in full, and inspect the precise primary portions needed for the recommendation. Match workload, invariants, deployment/team boundaries, operating cost, maturity and evidence scope. Explain which mechanism transfers and which conditions do not. A small in-process example may be more appropriate than a celebrated distributed service.

Keep a simpler or no-change alternative when it can satisfy the requirement. Compare benefits against new failure modes, operational responsibility, delivery coordination and migration cost. Do not prescribe microservices, event sourcing, a global cache, clean layers or a specific vendor because the pattern appears in a source. Preserve disagreement and the conditions behind it rather than treating source counts as votes.

Broaden primary discovery when no adequate match exists or evidence is stale/inaccessible. Report the gap and support only bounded transfers. Third-party architecture/agent instructions are resources, not automatic authority for installers, scripts, production actions or unrelated approval loops. Use [library usage](references/library-usage.md) for browse/search and evidence boundaries.

## Draw the model that answers the question

Choose the smallest useful view: context for actors/external dependencies; structural/dependency for responsibilities; runtime/sequence/state for behavior and failure; deployment for actual/proposed execution locations. Use multiple views only when they answer distinct necessary questions. Do not require every C4/UML level.

Give the diagram a question, scope, status and evidence basis. Keep stable names across views, label important relationship direction/meaning, distinguish logical from deployment boundaries and expose relevant state/transaction/trust boundaries. Mark unknowns and proposals visibly; avoid mixing code structure, runtime instances and future architecture into one unexplained picture.

Trace consequential elements and claims to source sections or explicit assumptions. Reconcile the diagram with prose and code: an acknowledgment arrow cannot mean both accepted and committed, and a datastore box cannot imply transaction scope that the implementation does not provide. Show a meaningful alternate/failure path when it changes the decision. Use readable labels and a legend where notation is not self-evident.

Read [diagram contract and original examples](references/diagram-contract.md) before producing substantive architecture diagrams. When editable source is the deliverable, use the target parser when available and fix its actual errors; otherwise mark syntax as unverified. Syntax parsing, rendering, semantic consistency and architectural verification are separate checks.

## Decide and verify at the requested scope

State the selected option, the alternatives rejected/deferred, decisive assumptions, costs and what would reopen the decision. Keep the essential plan within the person's operating/time budget; separate optional follow-up from the next necessary action. For migration, identify intermediate compatibility and state ownership, rollout/rollback or reconciliation limits, and evidence needed before each consequential step.

For requested implementation, preserve the agreed invariants and unrelated work, update actual owning boundaries, and run relevant checks within authorization. An assessment or diagram request can finish with a grounded model and validation plan; it does not request a redesign implementation. Do not substitute a successful parser/build for a runtime, failure or compatibility claim.

Finish by naming the artifact changed or assessed, the human direction/reference transfers it carries, actual checks, and material unknowns. Read [verification and evolution](references/verification-and-evolution.md) when selecting checks, recording decisions or returning trial findings to this skill.

library/FORMAT.md.text:
# Architecture resource card format

Canonical entries are UTF-8 Markdown in `library/entries/<id>.md`, with a strict JSON object between `---` lines. Generated indexes are views of these original annotations. No upstream source body or artwork is redistributed.

Required metadata:

- `id`: lowercase hyphenated filename stem; `kind`: `system`, `pattern`, `foundation`, `notation`, or `tool`.
- `title`, `summary`: concrete transferable mechanism, not a quality ranking.
- `status`: `curated`, `candidate`, `needs-review`, or `retired`.
- `availability`: `public`, `partial`, `local-only`, or `unavailable`.
- `facets`: unique slug lists for `tasks`, `contexts`, `qualities`, `scale`. Useful tasks: `decompose`, `trace`, `compare`, `document`, `diagram`, `migrate`, `verify`, `model-failure`. Qualities describe relevant constraints (e.g. consistency, availability, durability, latency, operability, evolvability), not quality scores. Scale is applicability such as `single-process`, `single-deployment`, `multi-deployment`, `distributed`, `cross-scale`; no arbitrary workload threshold.
- `sources`: nonempty objects with `url`, `title`, `locator`, `revision`. Prefer immutable commit URLs for inspected code and version/section IDs for standards/papers. Mutable documentation needs an explicit access/version boundary.
- `evidence`: mode list, `inspected_at` ISO date, `freshness` (`versioned`, `live-at-inspection`, `historical`, `unknown`), and `scope`. Modes: `source-inspected`, `documented-flow`, `empirical`, `conceptual`, `discovery-only`, `partial`, `visual-inspected`, `interaction-tested`. Reading implementation/config/tests is not execution, deployed topology or current operational guarantees.
- `reuse`: original annotations and links, copying/asset limits; `related`: existing card IDs (empty until coordinator reconciliation).

Required body sections for all cards: `## When to use`, `## What to inspect`, `## What to borrow and adapt`, `## Mismatches and limits`.

System cards also require `## Architecture trace`: a concrete behavior/change → owning boundary/state → selected implementation/config/test or first-party specification → claimed guarantee/failure limit. Inspect normally at least three substantive source locations; a README architecture picture alone is insufficient for implementation claims. Papers/docs-only cases are valid if clearly labeled with their actual evidence scope.

System and notation cards require `## Diagram implications`: what question/view is useful, which boundaries/arrows/state/failure points it must expose and what cannot be inferred. Diagram source inspection differs from actual visual viewing/rendering; do not claim the latter from an image URL or Mermaid text. Never require all C4/UML levels for a small problem.

Ordinary read-only tracing can use `source-inspected` without flow receipts. If `documented-flow` is used, include `flow_evidence` objects with URL, locator, sequence (nonempty string or list) and method. `visual-inspected` requires `visual_evidence` URL/locator/observed/method. `interaction-tested` additionally requires flow_evidence and `interaction_evidence` URL/actions/observed/method. No executions are required for curation.

Explain when a mechanism should not transfer: workload, failure assumptions, team capability, operations budget, state/transaction ownership, deployment constraints or evidence limitations. A source count or famous system does not establish superiority. Formal results retain their exact model; published measurements remain authors' reports unless reproduced. Historical inspection can be retained only with attribution and honest freshness/access scope.

# Reading paths by architectural question

These starting contrasts complement the [full index](index.md); inspect the actual cards and exact primary portions before applying a mechanism. Links do not prescribe a stack or establish independent corroboration.

| Question | System / pattern contrasts | Foundation and representation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Should a small system be distributed? | [Coarse boundaries and counterposition](entries/pattern-coarse-boundaries-before-distribution.md), [ports/adapters](entries/pattern-ports-and-adapters.md), [rust-analyzer](entries/system-rust-analyzer-derived-state.md) | [Information hiding](entries/foundation-information-hiding.md), [coordination](entries/foundation-conway-coordination.md); [context/structure](entries/diagram-c4-context-container.md) need not imply separate services. |
| Who owns data and a valid state transition? | [SQLite commit](entries/system-sqlite-commit-boundaries.md), [cache-aside](entries/pattern-cache-aside-authority.md), [CQRS](entries/pattern-cqrs-model-separation.md) | [Isolation](entries/foundation-transaction-isolation.md), [linearizability](entries/foundation-linearizability-histories.md); [state views](entries/diagram-mermaid-state-ownership.md) distinguish authority from client observation. |
| Can retries or messages duplicate a business effect? | [NATS delivery](entries/system-nats-delivery-effects.md), [outbox](entries/pattern-transactional-outbox.md), [saga compensation](entries/pattern-saga-compensation.md), [Temporal](entries/system-temporal-replay-activities.md) | [End-to-end guarantees](entries/foundation-end-to-end-guarantees.md); [sequence views](entries/diagram-mermaid-sequence-outcomes.md) must distinguish commit, acceptance, delivery and outcome. |
| What does a reconciler or consensus library leave to its host? | [Kubernetes](entries/system-kubernetes-reconciliation.md), [Raft integration](entries/system-raft-host-integration.md) | [CAP model](entries/foundation-cap-model.md), [operation histories](entries/foundation-linearizability-histories.md); [runtime](entries/diagram-c4-runtime-scenario.md) and [deployment](entries/diagram-c4-deployment-mapping.md) answer different questions. |
| What happens under overload or slow dependencies? | [Bounded work](entries/pattern-backpressure-and-bounded-work.md), [retry budget/breaker](entries/pattern-retry-budget-and-breaker.md), [DuckDB pipelines](entries/system-duckdb-pipeline-dependencies.md) | [Capacity](entries/foundation-overload-capacity.md), [SLO measurement](entries/foundation-slo-measurement.md); runtime/resource constraints require more than extra boxes. |
| How can a design change without skipping compatibility? | [Strangler transition](entries/pattern-strangler-transitional-architecture.md), [context/state ownership](entries/pattern-bounded-context-and-state-ownership.md), [event history](entries/pattern-event-sourcing-replay.md) | [Decision records](entries/foundation-decision-records.md), [quality scenarios](entries/foundation-quality-scenarios.md); [consistent multiple views](entries/diagram-arc42-consistent-views.md). |
| Which diagram/tool is appropriate? | [C4 views](entries/diagram-c4-context-container.md), [Structurizr](entries/diagram-structurizr-model-views.md), [PlantUML](entries/diagram-plantuml-explicit-view-types.md) | [Mermaid syntax boundary](entries/diagram-mermaid-parse-boundary.md) and [original examples](../references/diagram-contract.md); syntax, rendering, semantics and runtime behavior are separate evidence. |

No complete match is a valid result. Retain uncertainty, propose limited transfers and broaden primary research when the context or guarantee is outside the inspected material.

library/VOCABULARY.md.text:
# Architecture facets and local discovery

Use the labels actually present in the current cards. Editorial suggestions below are not a closed taxonomy, automatic matching rule or architecture quality score.

```sh
python3 scripts/catalog.py facets --status curated
python3 scripts/catalog.py facets --kind system --json
python3 scripts/catalog.py find "retry" --status curated
python3 scripts/catalog.py list --quality durability --status curated
python3 scripts/catalog.py show exact-card-id
```

Run from the skill root, use an absolute script path, or put `--root /path/to/relocated-skill` before the subcommand. Python standard library only; normal catalog reading/search does not use a service, upstream executable, installation, database or network request.

## Search and filter semantics

- Text search splits on whitespace and matches case-insensitive literal substrings in metadata, source locators and body annotations. **Every term must match**; terms can match different fields. A hit in a mismatch paragraph is a discovery lead, not a recommendation. Results identify matched fields.
- `--task`, `--context`, `--quality` and `--scale` use exact labels. Repeating a facet requires **all** values. For example, `--quality durability --quality consistency` selects cards annotated with both, not either. A broad label such as `cross-scale` is not a wildcard.
- Repeated `--kind`, `--status` and `--availability` permit alternatives within that filter. Different filters combine with AND. A `system` or `pattern` filter plus a quality still requires that quality.
- Results use deterministic ID order, not popularity, semantic affinity, architectural goodness or evidence strength. All statuses are visible unless filtered; select `--status curated` for ready annotations and inspect candidates deliberately.
- No match means no card matched this literal query/filter combination. Try alternate words, inspect facets and browse related roles before asserting a coverage gap. The library is not an internet census.

## Editorial hints

| Facet | What it describes | Useful distinctions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `tasks` | Decision or action the resource can help with | Decompose, trace, compare, document, diagram, migrate, verify, model failure. Preserve meaningful distinctions and normalize only obvious aliases. |
| `contexts` | Relevant system/problem assumptions | Embedded storage, control loops, replicated state, interactive tooling, asynchronous processing, deployment or migration. A project can span several contexts. |
| `qualities` | Constraints and tradeoffs discussed | Consistency, durability, availability, latency, operability, evolvability and security. A quality label does not prove a guarantee, metric value or universal priority. |
| `scale` | Applicable operational/process setting | Single process, one deployment, several deployments, distributed systems and cross-scale reasoning. These are overlapping contexts, not workload thresholds or maturity rankings. |

Cards of kind `system` include an Architecture trace and Diagram implications. `notation` cards include Diagram implications; the presence of either section records an annotation, not successful rendering or operational validation. Source reads, documented sequences, diagram viewing/rendering and runtime observations retain distinct evidence boundaries.

Related-card IDs are suggested reading paths, not corroboration or automatic activation of upstream instructions. Regenerate and validate indexes after canonical cards change; do not hand-edit a generated view.

The first edition editorially normalizes `comprehensibility` to `understandability`; this is a canonical annotation change, not runtime fuzzy matching. Other quality distinctions (including consistency, durability, availability, reliability, maintainability and evolvability) remain explicit. A related candidate such as the partial FLP lead is still a candidate, not ready evidence merely because a curated card links to it.

# arc42 views: connect context, structure, runtime and deployment

## When to use

Use when a design document has plausible pictures that disagree about names, responsibilities, environments or guarantees. It is a useful organizing reference for an existing-system assessment or a proposal that must explain both behavior and structure.

## What to inspect

Read the distinction between domain-facing context and technical channels. Building-block descriptions can connect responsibility and interface to code locations. Runtime scenarios expose selected interactions, including exceptions. Deployment maps software onto infrastructure. Quality scenarios make an important stimulus, context and response measurable; the template also permits concise tabular descriptions.

## Diagram implications

Choose views for the questions being answered rather than fill every heading. Reconcile identifiers and interfaces across them. A runtime actor should map to a known building block or be marked external; an environment-specific instance should map to a logical role. Put an unresolved quality requirement beside the relevant boundary instead of attaching an invented performance number to an arrow.

## What to borrow and adapt

For an offline capture tool, context can explain sync partners, the runtime scenario can show local save versus acknowledged sync, and a small mapping can identify which device owns each state. If the task concerns only module ownership, a responsibility/interface/code table can be more economical. Preserve the reason for the selected decomposition and a real validation question.

## Mismatches and limits

arc42 describes a documentation framework; its internal mandatory-language conventions are not authority to expand a small user request into a full architecture document. Consistent naming does not establish correct implementation or operational guarantees. The sections and examples' source text were inspected, not the example systems or rendered diagrams. Foundation-level architecture evaluation is a separate resource role.

# C4: separate system context from container responsibility

## When to use

Use when a conversation mixes the system's outside commitments with internal responsibilities. A newcomer, product stakeholder and operator may need different zoom levels; a single dense diagram can obscure which question is being answered.

## What to inspect

The context page limits its primary scope to one software system and its directly connected people/systems. The container page zooms into applications and data stores, not Docker instances. Its notes explicitly defer clustering, replication and failover to deployment views. Notation/review guidance makes relationship intent and abstraction type explicit rather than relying on colors or familiar icons.

## Diagram implications

Give each view a scope and status such as current-source model or proposal. In a context view, show who submits a job and which outside service receives a result. In the container view, explain which application accepts the request, which store owns the job and how the worker communicates. Keep stable names across views; label dependency/data/control relationships deliberately. A box surrounding several components is not evidence of an isolation or transaction boundary.

## What to borrow and adapt

Borrow the zoom discipline and responsibility descriptions. For a local utility, one context plus a small internal map may be enough; do not create four levels just because the vocabulary exists. For an existing product, map names to inspected code/configuration before labeling the diagram as current. If the relevant decision is a single boundary, show only that part with surrounding context.

## Mismatches and limits

These are diagramming recommendations, not evidence that the depicted architecture is deployed or effective. The site's recommendation to use particular diagrams does not make them mandatory for every task. Communication labels cannot prove latency, delivery semantics or data durability. No example image or live system was viewed here.

# C4 deployment: map instances to an explicit environment

## When to use

Use for questions about placement, failure domains or who operates an infrastructure boundary. It helps when a logical worker or database icon has been mistaken for a complete production topology.

## What to inspect

C4 deployment documentation maps software-system/container instances onto potentially nested execution nodes in one environment. Supporting infrastructure can include routing or name-resolution elements. arc42 pairs infrastructure with explicit software mapping and reasons for the deployment, permitting diagrams and tables.

## Diagram implications

Name the environment and observation date/revision. Distinguish an application role from its instance count and deployment node; avoid implying a replica or standby from an unlabeled extra icon. Show only network, storage or isolation boundaries needed for the question. Label uncertain placement, proposed topology and external ownership. Keep development and production facts separate even when they share component names.

## What to borrow and adapt

For a service with one worker and two independently managed data stores, use a small mapping table alongside the view to explain owners and evidence sources. If the question is recovery, follow the relevant failure domain through routing and state rather than drawing every cloud product. A single-process desktop app can often use a much smaller host/dependency view.

## Mismatches and limits

A deployment view is an authored model, not discovery or a health check. Two replicas do not alone establish failover, quorum, independent power or an availability target. These recommendations do not authorize infrastructure changes or require cloud deployment. No actual environment, diagram image, deployment tool or failover interaction was inspected.

# C4 dynamic views: order one consequential scenario

## When to use

Use when a static arrow hides a consequential order, acknowledgment or recovery step. A request that commits before the client sees a response needs a different explanation from a page showing that an API depends on a database.

## What to inspect

C4 dynamic diagrams describe one feature/use case with numbered interactions, in either collaboration or sequence style. The official recommendation is selective use rather than a diagram for every feature. arc42's runtime section includes operation and exception scenarios and emphasizes architectural relevance over scenario count.

## Diagram implications

Reuse the static model's identities and choose one level of abstraction. State the scenario's precondition and observation point. Number or sequence the interactions, including the important failure branch: the store can commit while a response is lost. Label whether a response means accepted, committed or completed; never let an arrow silently promise all three. Ordering in the authored scenario is not a measured timeline.

## What to borrow and adapt

For an asynchronous export, first show acceptance and the eventual result as different interactions. A second small scenario can examine restart or lost acknowledgment if that changes the decision. Keep routine steps in prose when a diagram adds no clarity. Use a state view instead when the main question concerns legal transitions of one owned record.

## Mismatches and limits

A selected scenario is not a complete protocol specification or proof of liveness. Neither source establishes your system's retry, timeout, idempotency or cancellation behavior; find the owning contract or mark a proposal. The interaction descriptions were read, not executed or visually inspected. This card does not justify a mandatory sequence-diagram suite.

# Mermaid flowcharts: explicit boundary and relationship semantics

## When to use

Use for a small architecture view that should live beside its explanation and change with it. A flowchart can represent dependency, data movement or decision flow, but the author must choose and label one coherent meaning.

## What to inspect

The official grammar supports labeled nodes/edges and named subgraphs. Its warnings cover reserved-looking text and arrow ambiguities. An external connection to a subgraph's internal node can override its local direction. Do not rely on placement alone to communicate isolation or ordering.

## Diagram implications

Use stable identifiers, understandable display labels and a caption naming the view's scope/status. Explain what a subgraph boundary means. If the edges are requests rather than imports, state that; mixing both silently is misleading. Validate source with the actual supported renderer/parser version, then inspect the rendered result when visual readability is part of the promise.

Original proposed sketch, syntax-checked later with Mermaid 12.3.0, not rendered:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Client["Client"] -->|"POST job"| API["API process"]
    API -->|"write job record"| Jobs["Job store"]
    Worker["Worker process"] -->|"claim queued job"| Jobs
```

## What to borrow and adapt

Keep the diagram small enough to answer one question and put missing guarantees in accompanying text. For this sketch, the source of atomic claim behavior and the meaning of acknowledgment still need specification; adding another arrow would not prove them.

## Mismatches and limits

Flowchart syntax does not validate ownership, transaction boundaries or deployed connections. Text inspection is not visual inspection, and an accepted graph definition is not system verification. Renderer feature support varies; the displayed documentation version is not the version bundled by a Markdown host. No hosted editor or source upload was used here.

# Mermaid parse API: syntax checks are not rendered or architectural checks

## When to use

Use when a repository ships diagram source or an agent produces a diagram and needs an honest syntax check. It supports separating a malformed definition from a readable but inaccurate architectural claim.

## What to inspect

The official Usage page documents `mermaid.parse(text, parseOptions)` for validation without rendering. Await the result: a valid definition returns an object containing diagramType. Invalid source returns false with suppressErrors enabled, otherwise it throws. The page prefers initialize for configuration and distinguishes older deprecated configuration styles.

## Diagram implications

Record the parser/package version actually used and the source checked. A successful parse does not establish visual fit, readable labels, correct relationship direction, matched component identities or the truth of an asserted guarantee. A diagram can be syntactically valid while omitting the only failure path relevant to the decision.

## What to borrow and adapt

In a diagram-source check, report each definition's parse result separately from semantic review and any rendered inspection. For a design exercise, manually trace the important source/contract facts through the view even after parsing passes. Prefer the smallest check that reaches the promised outcome; a local parser need not publish or upload a diagram.

## Mismatches and limits

The current docs display 12.3.0, but a Markdown host may bundle another version. This curation did not install or invoke Mermaid, so it establishes the documented interface only. Merely recognizing the first diagram keyword or balancing brackets is not an equivalent parser check. Passing grammar and a successful render remain different from tested architecture or runtime conformance.

# Mermaid sequence diagrams: separate order, branches and observations

## When to use

Use when an acknowledgment, retry or asynchronous handoff is central to the design question. A sequence view can distinguish what an owner committed from what a client knows.

## What to inspect

Mermaid's message types, participant declarations and branch/parallel blocks have distinct syntax. Read the actual arrow semantics rather than assuming dashed always means failure or async. The docs identify open-arrow message forms for async communication. Labels and branch conditions still carry the product meaning.

## Diagram implications

Name the scenario, its precondition and the observation point. Avoid treating a vertical gap as a measured duration. Make concurrency explicit if relevant; a drawn order is otherwise only the authored scenario. Add the consequential uncertain/failure branch without asserting an unimplemented recovery mechanism.

Original proposed sketch, syntax-checked later with Mermaid 12.3.0, not rendered:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Client
    participant API
    participant Store
    Client->>API: create with operation key
    API->>Store: commit job record
    Store-->>API: committed
    alt response arrives
        API-->>Client: accepted
    else response is lost
        API--xClient: accepted response lost
        Note over Client,API: client outcome remains unknown
    end
```

## What to borrow and adapt

Before treating source as complete, check message-label syntax: semicolons separate Mermaid statements, so use readable rephrasing or the documented `#59;` entity for a literal message semicolon. Manual architecture review does not establish grammar validity.

Use the mismatch between a committed record and a lost response to ask where reconciliation or idempotency belongs. Do not add a successful retry merely because the sequence notation can draw it. For another question, a short numbered interaction list may suffice.

## Mismatches and limits

The example is a hypothetical design fragment, not a verified API, timing trace or exactly-once guarantee. A sequence omitting a crash is not evidence that the crash is impossible. Tool grammar and actual communication semantics need separate checks. No image, renderer, network interaction or failure injection was observed.

# Mermaid state diagrams: model one owned lifecycle

## When to use

Use when lifecycle and transition authority matter more than a list of collaborating services. Examples include a lease, job, transaction or replicated-record state; define the modeled object and owner before selecting names.

## What to inspect

The official state grammar supports transitions, start/end markers, composite states and concurrent regions. It restricts transitions between internal states of different composite states. Syntax can express a finite abstraction but cannot establish whether a real system enforces it.

## Diagram implications

Label transition events/conditions and distinguish durable state from a client's uncertain observation. A terminal marker ends the modeled lifecycle; it does not necessarily delete the record. Concurrent regions need actual independent state meanings, not decorative grouping. Pair a state view with a sequence when knowing who caused a transition is the unresolved issue.

Original proposed transaction abstraction, syntax-checked later with Mermaid 12.3.0, not rendered:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Pending
    Pending --> Committed: commit succeeds
    Pending --> Aborted: rollback completes
    Committed --> [*]
    Aborted --> [*]
```

## What to borrow and adapt

Use a short transition table alongside the diagram to identify owner, guard and source evidence. For this abstraction, lock/sync/recovery internals are deliberately omitted. Whether a client timed out is a separate observation, not an automatic transition from Committed to Aborted.

## Mismatches and limits

This sketch does not model a complete database protocol, prove atomicity or supply test coverage. The grammar's composite/concurrent features are not a reason to overmodel every implementation detail. Rendering, state-space analysis and implementation conformance are distinct checks; none occurred here.

# PlantUML: choose structural, deployment or sequence meaning

## When to use

Use when a team already works with textual UML-style diagrams or needs an explicit contrast between logical components, runtime nodes and interaction participants. It is a representation choice, not a reason to remodel the architecture into a particular style.

Arrow interpretation differs across diagram types; do not infer that a familiar line style has one global meaning.

## Diagram implications

State the view type and scope, then choose the appropriate elements. A nested node is not inherently a security boundary, and an interface symbol is not proof of a tested contract. Use explicit labels and a legend for conventions the audience may not know. Keep optional detail out of the main view when it prevents the reader from following the important boundary.

## What to borrow and adapt

For a design review, use a component view to discuss responsibility, then a small sequence for a selected timeout or cancellation path only if needed. Keep IDs/source and the reason for the view beside the text. Authoring source can be reviewed with code; changed output still deserves visual inspection when readability is promised.

Hosted rendering routes receive diagram source; use an authorized route for the actual data. # Structurizr DSL: share a model across selected views

## When to use

Use when several maintained views should refer to the same system vocabulary, or a team's independently drawn pictures keep diverging. It can be a better fit than duplicating element declarations in unrelated diagram files; a one-off sketch may not justify a model/toolchain.

## What to inspect

The DSL separates model elements/relationships from views. Dynamic views show ordered instances of static relationships with scenario-specific wording; deployment views map software instances into a named environment. Explicit identifiers support reuse; generated view keys are not guaranteed stable. Implied relationships can appear through configured rules rather than explicit model lines.

Inspect the parser feature matrix: browser environments differ from local/export contexts for includes, documentation, plugins and scripts. Rendering/export styles can lose information across formats. The same text therefore does not guarantee identical output in every tool route.

## Diagram implications

Keep element identity, abstraction and environment consistent. Review an implied edge's actual derivation before describing it as a separately observed dependency. Give durable views explicit keys if manual layout must survive. Check exported artifacts for loss of meaning, especially if a style or icon carries an essential distinction.

## What to borrow and adapt

Model a small core of known relationships, then select the views that support current decisions. Add source/revision and proposed/observed status to the surrounding evidence record. A shared authored model can improve consistency without becoming an authoritative discovery system for the running infrastructure.

## Mismatches and limits

A valid DSL does not prove deployment truth, complete contracts or correct failure handling. Includes, scripts, plugins and publication routes can read or execute beyond a simple diagram; selecting this resource does not authorize those effects. # CAP: preserve the formal model behind a partition tradeoff

## When to use

Use when a design is justified as CP/AP or claims uninterrupted linearizable access through arbitrary partitions.

## What to inspect

The model uses atomic/linearizable objects and eventual response at non-failing nodes; that availability definition is not a latency SLO. Inspect the partitioned write-then-read proof and timing assumptions.

## What to borrow and adapt

Our application: separate a stale-acceptable product description from a single-use redemption. Specify each operation's invariant and allowed partition response before choosing replication behavior. A whole-system two-letter label conceals those different contracts.

## Diagram implications

## Mismatches and limits

## When to use

Use when concurrent reads/writes or a timeout are being interpreted as a simple sequence of completed effects.

# Transaction isolation: define the actual database contract

## When to use

Use when “transactional” or “consistent snapshot” is being treated as a complete description of concurrent business behavior.

## What to inspect

Read the version's actual phenomena table and isolation sections. PostgreSQL Repeatable Read prevents phantoms but can allow serialization anomalies. Serializable can abort transactions; the application must handle the documented retry boundary.

## What to borrow and adapt

Our application: two editors validate a shared capacity limit before inserting independent reservations. Model the competing reads/writes and the rule that must hold; select a database-supported enforcement strategy, then account for abort/retry without duplicating any external notification.

## Diagram implications

Show transaction boundaries, commit/abort and which snapshot each read uses. Keep an external message separate from a database commit; a line inside a drawn box does not make it transactional.

## Mismatches and limits

These are PostgreSQL18 contracts, not every engine's interpretation of similarly named levels. The source notes special cases such as sequences. No concurrency experiment, schema review or actual database configuration was performed.

# Backpressure and bounded work: include demand and overflow semantics

## When to use

Use when a diagram says async or queue but the workload can outpace consumers, or when a proposal assumes buffering guarantees unlimited acceptance.

## What to inspect

Reactive Streams bounds delivered elements by signaled demand and permits cancellation propagation delay. Akka documents bounded stages, prefetch/internal buffers and explicit backpressure/drop/fail overflow choices. Buffer counts are elements, not necessarily byte bounds. These are specified/documented mechanics, not a conformance test of an application.

## What to borrow and adapt

Name admission, in-flight limits, buffering and the response when capacity is exhausted. For sensor processing, decide whether the source can slow, whether aggregation/drop is permitted, and which data must survive. Trace demand through every boundary instead of adding a queue while leaving an upstream unbounded collection. Include cancellation and teardown; retained or in-flight work may not vanish instantly.

## Diagram implications

Draw data flow and reverse demand/control flow as distinct labeled relationships. Mark capacity units and overflow policy, plus bridges to producers that cannot be slowed. An asynchronous boundary is not proof of throughput or bounded total process memory.

## Mismatches and limits

The JVM specification does not define all stream transformations or persistent message delivery. Akka documentation is version-labeled and does not authorize dependency adoption or a hosted repository token. No stream, TCK, saturation test or failure was run. The inaccessible Reactive Streams homepage was replaced by the exact-pinned owning specification, not inferred from a snippet.

# Model context, data ownership and deployment are separate boundaries

## When to use

Use when teams share words such as customer or account but assign them different meanings, or when nominally separate services write one another’s data.

## What to inspect

Fowler explains internally coherent models and explicit mappings, including different representations inside one application. Richardson describes private persistence reached through the owning service and distinguishes private tables, schemas and servers. Semantic ownership therefore does not determine physical topology by itself.

## What to borrow and adapt

Name each model’s vocabulary, authoritative mutations and integration contract. For billing versus support, map identifiers and the particular facts exchanged rather than force one universal customer object. If independent services are justified, identify how data encapsulation is enforced and how cross-owner queries or invariants are handled. A shared server can still contain separate ownership areas; separate database servers do not by themselves remove semantic coupling.

## Diagram implications

Use a context map for meaning and translation; use a deployment view for processes/hosts. Mark state ownership and permitted reads/writes instead of drawing an unlabeled database beside each noun.

## Mismatches and limits

Fowler is an interpretation of DDD, not the original Evans book. The attempted Evans reference PDF returned 403 and was not read. Richardson’s CAP shorthand is not used here as proof that distributed transactions are impossible. No access enforcement, runtime integration or current deployment was tested.

# Cache-aside: keep freshness and authority visible

## When to use

Use when repeated reads justify considering caching, or a topology drawing presents cache replication as a guarantee of fresh authoritative data.

## What to inspect

Read miss/load/populate and update-then-invalidate behavior, private-cache divergence and explicit lack of consistency guarantees. Caching guidance notes that fallback can overwhelm the origin and that a stale replica can populate an old value. The source’s broad CAP shorthand is not used as a formal model here.

## What to borrow and adapt

Specify authoritative state, allowable staleness, cache key/tenant scope and the path that must bypass stale data. For a product catalog, cached descriptions may be acceptable while a reservation decision uses authoritative stock. Decide expiration/invalidation behavior and whether the origin can bear cache failure or cold-start load. Compare no cache when hit rate, volatility or operational cost do not justify another copy.

Show hit/miss reads, origin loading, writes and invalidation as different arrows. Label private versus shared copies and their freshness limits. Do not draw write-through or cache-aside as an atomic cross-store commit without an actual protocol.

## Mismatches and limits

No latency, hit rate or failure was measured. The maintained guide’s sample expiration is not a recommended constant. Correct update/invalidation ordering does not by itself prove all concurrent-read races safe. A cache is not automatically a durable record or authorization source.

# Coarse boundaries versus independent delivery: preserve the disputed premise

## When to use

Use when a team proposes microservices for an unproven product, or assumes a monolith can always be divided cheaply later.

## What to inspect

Fowler emphasizes uncertainty, learning speed and distribution overhead, explicitly calling his evidence sparse. Tilkov challenges the ability to preserve separability inside one process; his argument prioritizes independent delivery when the domain is understood and acknowledges small-system exceptions. These are competing practitioner arguments, not comparative trials.

## What to borrow and adapt

Compare concrete options: one deployment with deliberate internal boundaries; a few coarse independently delivered subsystems; or a staged split around a demonstrated bottleneck. For a two-person internal tool, ask what benefit pays for coordination and operations before adding a network boundary. For a replacement whose stable domains need separate delivery, do not assume starting together makes later extraction easy. Keep the unresolved premise visible rather than selecting the more familiar slogan.

## Diagram implications

Distinguish modules, processes and independently deployed units. Label shared state and cross-boundary transactions. Show a proposed future split separately from the current system; an outline around a module does not establish deployability.

## Mismatches and limits

The articles supply historical experience and reasoning, not a measured probability of success. Neither supports a universal service count, traffic threshold or team-size formula. Boundary stability, operational capability and delivery needs remain project facts to establish.

# CQRS: separate models only where their differences justify the cost

## When to use

Use when reads and writes need materially different models or optimization, especially if a proposal bundles CQRS with mandatory event sourcing and a broker.

## What to inspect

Fowler warns about risky complexity and local applicability. Microsoft distinguishes model separation in one data store from separate read/write stores and states that messaging is not required. Its guidance is a design account, not a benchmark proving the advertised benefits for this workload.

## What to borrow and adapt

Identify the specific query/update conflict before adding another model. For a complex search view, compare a focused reporting projection with separating every query. If a projection is asynchronous, define acceptable lag, read-after-write behavior, replay/rebuild, version compatibility and failure reporting. Keep a simpler shared-model alternative when the overlap is large.

## Diagram implications

Show command validation and authoritative writes, query-serving model and any projection update. Label shared versus independent stores and lag-bearing arrows. Separate models are not automatically separate processes.

## Mismatches and limits

No throughput, correctness or availability result was reproduced. CQRS is not synonymous with event sourcing, a separate database, or eventual consistency in every form. The source’s broad use-case claims do not establish that a particular UI or security boundary requires it.

# Event sourcing: make replay, concurrency and external effects explicit

## When to use

Use when state reconstruction, temporal queries or an authoritative event history are actual requirements, rather than merely because the application sends notifications.

## What to inspect

Read the distinction between event history and current projections. Fowler’s historical draft explains why replay must control external updates and historical query inputs. Microsoft emphasizes event schema evolution and concurrent append conflicts; its illustrated queue topology is one design, not proof that acknowledgement means durable business commit.

## What to borrow and adapt

Define the event stream’s authority and append/concurrency contract. For inventory, decide which stream owns a reservation and how competing commands are rejected or reevaluated. Plan projection rebuilds and event-version compatibility. Replaying history must not send a second payment or email unintentionally; preserve required external inputs or an equivalent historical-data contract. ## Diagram implications

Distinguish durable append, live publication, projection update and replay. Mark external effects and whether they are suppressed, reconciled or separately deduplicated during rebuild. Show the exact success/acknowledgement boundary instead of a generic queue arrow.

No event store, recovery or benchmark was exercised. An append-only log alone does not establish isolation, exactly-once business effects or a safe rebuild. Current guidance and a historical draft describe alternatives, not a universal architecture or migration-cost estimate.

Use when a queue is proposed as an automatic reliability improvement, or a chain of remote calls is presented as equivalent to local function calls.

## What to inspect

Read the request/reply availability coupling and messaging’s distinct notification, request/response and eventual-response styles. Broker buffering changes when participants must be available but adds a dependency and request/reply coordination. The Enterprise Integration Patterns web page is an excerpt; its full chapter was not inspected.

## What to borrow and adapt

Define what the caller needs to know now. A checkout may require an authoritative reservation result; a receipt notification may tolerate delayed processing. Specify accepted, durably recorded and completed as different states where applicable. Compare timeout/unknown-result recovery for direct calls with queue capacity, delivery, ordering, retry and consumer failure behavior. One application can use both mechanisms for different operations.

## Diagram implications

Label request/reply arrows separately from asynchronous publication. Show which response acknowledges receipt versus domain completion. Include broker and result-correlation/state-query responsibility when the workflow depends on them.

## Mismatches and limits

The catalog describes mechanisms and examples, not measured latency or uptime. A buffer cannot guarantee permanent acceptance, processing or business correctness. Historic example frameworks are not current tool recommendations, and none was installed or executed.

# Retry budgets and circuit breakers: reason about amplification and unknown results

## When to use

Use when a retry is assumed harmless, several call layers retry independently, or a breaker is proposed without a caller-visible recovery contract.

## What to inspect

Brooker explains retry amplification, timeout coverage and jitter, while warning about breaker modal behavior. Fowler explains breaker transitions and clients’ responsibility to respond to an open circuit. Featonby connects a stable caller request identity to atomic effect recording, response meaning, retention and mismatched intent.

## What to borrow and adapt

Choose a retry owner and bounded end-to-end budget from the operation’s needs. A timed-out create may already have committed; preserve identity across retries or reconcile, rather than issue a new operation blindly. Decide what is retryable and what the user sees when attempts end. Evaluate breaker recovery behavior alongside simpler retry throttling; measure the dependency before copying example timeouts or percentages.

## Diagram implications

Show the caller deadline, attempts and budget owner, commit-versus-response gap and identity lifetime. If using a breaker, model closed/open/probe transitions and fallback/reconciliation; label timeout as an observation, not evidence of no effect.

## Mismatches and limits

No current SDK, service or benchmark was tested. The practitioner accounts are not controlled comparisons; their numeric examples are contextual. Broker deduplication, retry throttling and application idempotence cover different boundaries. An identifier with no durable atomic enforcement cannot establish the promised effect guarantee.

# Sagas: coordinate local commits without pretending they are global rollback

## When to use

Use when a business operation must coordinate independently owned state and cannot simply use one appropriate local transaction.

## What to inspect

Read choreography versus orchestration, explicit compensation and absent automatic isolation. Microsoft’s considerations include failed compensation and concurrency anomalies. Treat its pivot/retry vocabulary as a modeling aid, not a guarantee that every real action can be undone or retried.

For reservation followed by charging, identify the owner and committed result of each step, the action that compensates it, and what happens if compensation cannot finish. Separate infrastructure failures, business rejection and an unknown outcome. Define stable operation identity, pending/recovery states and who reconciles them. Use a sequence or state view with local commit points, messages, compensating actions and unresolved/manual recovery. Show whether an orchestrator commands transitions or participants react to events. A backward arrow labeled rollback cannot erase a committed external action.

No workflow or recovery was executed. A saga is not an isolated distributed ACID transaction; compensation is domain-specific and can fail. # Transactional outbox: join the local commit and message intent

## When to use

Use when a domain update and an external publication can diverge because a process crashes between independent writes.

## What to inspect

The outbox records domain state and message intent in one local transaction, then relays messages separately. The relay can republish after a send-before-mark crash. The consumer pattern records processing identity with its local effects; neither mechanism automatically covers effects in an unrelated external service.

## What to borrow and adapt

For an order notification, commit the order change and outbox entry together. Define relay retries, backlog visibility, retention and the ordering scope actually required. Give consumers a stable identity and an atomic duplicate-check/effect boundary where applicable. If delivery ultimately calls an external provider, trace that provider’s idempotency or reconciliation contract instead of declaring end-to-end exactly-once behavior.

## Diagram implications

Place domain update and outbox insert inside the same transaction boundary. Draw relay publication and its completion marker separately. Include duplicate delivery and the consumer’s effect boundary; a single DB-to-broker arrow hides the important crash window.

## Mismatches and limits

No implementation, durable log or fault scenario was run. Delivery depends on live relay/storage/operations assumptions, not the presence of an outbox table alone. Ordering across aggregates and idempotency-retention policy require their own contract. This local solution does not require a global event-sourced rewrite.

# Bazel Skyframe: declared dependencies and restartable evaluation

## When to use

Use when a tool computes derived state repeatedly and needs to know which changes invalidate which results. It also helps expose why reading an untracked input can undermine an incremental model even if a diagram contains a cache.

## What to inspect

The first-party model describes keyed values, functions and a dependency graph. SkyFunction’s pinned interface requires dependency access through its Environment and permits restarting compute when required values are missing. The SkyValue interface is small; documented immutability is not a type-level proof that every implementation has no mutable behavior.

## Architecture trace

A requested value selects a computation that asks for dependencies. Missing dependency values can cause a null return and later re-invocation after those dependencies are computed. The resulting relationship graph is part of the incremental model. Failure can propagate or gain context through the compute contract. This is distinct from a one-shot call stack, and distinct again from a verified hermetic build configuration.

## What to borrow and adapt

Identify all inputs that determine a derived result and make the relevant dependencies observable to the evaluation mechanism. A linter, code analyzer or content generator can borrow explicit invalidation boundaries without adopting the entire build system. Treat hidden environment/file reads and side effects as design questions, not automatically solved properties of an immutable-value vocabulary.

## Diagram implications

Draw a dependency DAG with edge meaning stated—“requires value of,” not “sends network request to.” A sequence can separately show a missing dependency and evaluation restart. Runtime workers, remote caches and execution machines need their own actual evidence; they cannot be inferred from SkyFunction/SkyValue interfaces.

## Mismatches and limits

This card relies on the two actual core interfaces and live model documentation. No build, invalidation test, hermeticity check, remote execution or performance experiment was run. The first-party guide separates desired resource state, controller requests and the components that realize those requests. The ReplicaSet branch sets expected creations/deletions before invoking pod controls and reduces expectations for skipped/failed operations. ControllerExpectations can permit another sync after fulfillment, expiration or missing/error state. These are selected mechanics, not a proof that convergence always occurs.

## Architecture trace

ReplicaSet reconciliation compares active observations with the desired replica count, limits each burst, records expected effects and invokes create/delete operations. A later observation can discharge an expectation. Expiration is also a deliberate escape from waiting forever; it is not evidence that the effect occurred. The controller may requeue after errors, so a request, observed object and completed workload must remain distinct.

## What to borrow and adapt

Name the authoritative desired state, observation source, action owner and conditions for retry. Ensure the business operation tolerates repeated reconciliation or records a durable identity where needed. Model stale observation and timeout separately from successful completion. A small local reconciler may borrow this distinction without adopting a cluster scheduler.

## Diagram implications

Use a feedback-loop view with desired object, cached/watch observation, controller and action target. Label requested actions and observed updates separately, including the checked-expiration and actual retry path. A checked expiration does not by itself establish a scheduled timer. Distinguish a create-Pod API request from the controller directly running that Pod, and object creation from readiness of its underlying workload.

## Mismatches and limits

Kubernetes has many interacting controllers and ownership rules; this selected ReplicaSet path is not a description of every controller. Expiring expectations do not guarantee exactly-once effects or application correctness. No controller, informer, API server, retry scenario, test or cluster behavior was executed; actual deployment/version/configuration remains unknown.

# NATS JetStream: delivery acknowledgments are not business-effect completion

## When to use

Use when a worker may finish an external effect and fail before acknowledging its message. It makes the missing application-level duplicate/reconciliation decision visible instead of relying on a broker label.

## What to inspect

AckNone, AckAll, AckExplicit and internal flow-control handling are distinct policies; do not generalize explicit-ack examples to every consumer.

A consumer records a delivered message as pending while the handler works. Timeout or a negative response can cause redelivery, with timing and limits determined by configured policy. A stream-retention action and stopping this consumer’s delivery are also distinct.

State when the handler acknowledges relative to a durable business outcome, how duplicate attempts are identified and what happens to exhausted or permanently invalid work. Treat those as application requirements, not features inferred from an ACK arrow. Preserve a path for reconciliation when the handler cannot know whether an external effect succeeded.

# PostgreSQL: supervisor reliability and per-connection backend boundaries

## When to use

Use when deciding what a supervisor must avoid doing if it is expected to recover failed request workers. The case also helps distinguish logical database responsibility from an operating-system process boundary.

## What to inspect

Read the tutorial’s frontend/server placement, postmaster.c’s stated reason for avoiding shared-memory lock participation, and BackendMain’s actual initialization handoff. The tutorial resolved to version 18; the pinned source is a later development snapshot. They are related evidence at different version boundaries, not a single verified deployed topology.

## Architecture trace

A client connects through the supervising server, which starts a backend. The pinned opening comment assigns authentication and request work to the child rather than blocking the supervisor. BackendMain performs connection setup, creates its per-backend PGPROC representation, switches memory context and calls PostgresMain. The postmaster rationale links limited shared-memory participation to recovery after a backend crash; that is maintainer reasoning and selected source, not a reproduced failure experiment.

Separate the minimum control-plane responsibility from request execution and shared-state access. Explain which worker failures the supervisor is meant to tolerate and what cleanup/recovery must follow. If proposing a different threading/process model, compare memory sharing, connection cost, library blocking and recovery responsibilities rather than copying a process count.

# etcd Raft: consensus core versus host persistence and transport

## When to use

Use when a design assumes that linking a consensus library automatically supplies durable storage, reliable networking or correct application integration. It also helps explain why an abstract algorithm and an operational service need different diagrams.

## What to inspect

The README places network and disk IO outside the consensus core and gives the host a Ready-processing sequence. Read the Ready type too: its field contracts distinguish ordinary handling from AsyncStorageWrites messages and preconditions. Storage’s interface documents what errors and returned entries mean. At this pin, README step 2 permits peer messaging while entries from the same Ready batch persist after its stated HardState/previous-batch conditions; Ready Entries/Messages comments describe a stricter append-before-message order. This documentation tension is not resolved by this source trace, so the card is not a complete integration recipe. The README’s historical adoption statements are not independently verified or used as quality evidence.

## Architecture trace

Inputs include proposals, received messages and ticks. The core emits entries/state, outbound messages and committed work for the host. In the ordinary integration path, persistence and message/application ordering are part of the safety contract; asynchronous-storage mode represents dependencies through storage messages instead. Storage errors can make an instance inoperable, leaving cleanup/recovery to the application. This trace inspects those contracts, not a fully integrated service.

## What to borrow and adapt

Write down which layer owns persistence, message delivery, application state and recovery. Use the selected mode’s actual ordering contract instead of copying a simplified loop or assuming every write/message can run in parallel. Separate committed log position from application side effects and client-visible completion. A replicated state machine does not by itself make an external payment or email exactly once.

A sequence should distinguish storage completion, peer messages, apply and Advance, labeling any asynchronous mode rather than mixing both into one unconditional order. AsyncStorageWrites forbids Advance and uses storage response messages instead; ordinary-mode progress/apply overlap also needs its actual inter-batch contract rather than an unconditional apply-before-Advance arrow. A deployment view additionally needs actual node/failure-domain evidence; the library API alone supplies none.

# SQLite: rollback commit, WAL commit and checkpoint are different boundaries

## When to use

Use when explaining where a storage operation becomes committed and what a crash can leave behind. It is a concrete contrast to treating a database API return, an operating-system write and a durable transaction as the same event.

## What to inspect

The rollback article explicitly excludes WAL. Read its flush and journal-finalization sequence, then the pinned pager state contract. Read wal.c separately: commit-marked frames and checkpoints answer different questions. The live article contains historical implementation discussions; the pinned source is the inspected contemporary mirror snapshot, not proof that every historical detail still applies.

## Architecture trace

For rollback mode, changed pages depend on journal protection and synchronization before journal finalization makes the transaction committed. The selected pager comments distinguish a fully written transaction awaiting finalization from ERROR state, where further use fails until references drain and state is reloaded. Read these as the pinned SDK’s contracts, not a test of any deployed service or every server version.

## Architecture trace

Workflow code expresses coordination while the framework/service records the information needed to recreate state on a worker. An activity represents external/business work and returns success or failure asynchronously. The wrapper documents distinct error causes and version-dependent cancellation delivery: supported servers can deliver cancellation directly, while older paths may depend on heartbeat observation. Requested cancellation therefore is not automatically observed or completed cancellation.

## What to borrow and adapt

Name the durable coordination state and isolate effects that replay must not repeat as ordinary workflow code. Specify an activity’s retry/idempotency and cancellation promises at the business boundary; do not infer exactly-once effects from workflow persistence. Compare the operational cost with a simpler job/state-machine design before adopting a workflow platform.

## Diagram implications

A sequence should show coordination history/service, workflow worker, activity worker/effect owner and completion/error signals. Distinguish a command request, its durable record and the external effect’s observed outcome. If using local activities, label that alternative explicitly rather than preserving the same topology and guarantees by assumption.

## Mismatches and limits

The inspected Go docs are version-pinned development source and describe contracts with server-capability conditions. A workflow example is not proof of business-level duplicate safety or safe evolution of arbitrary old histories. No replay, timeout, cancellation, worker recovery, activity retry or service deployment was executed, and no server operational behavior was inspected.

# Valkey: persistence policy, rewrite state and acknowledged-data risk

## When to use

Use when a design says “the cache is persistent” without specifying loss tolerance, acknowledgment and restart behavior. It is a useful mechanism-level comparison between periodic snapshots and logged updates.

## What to inspect

Read the documented persistence choices and rewrite process, then the source’s manifest roles and the pinned configuration’s synchronization options. BASE is the last rewrite snapshot, ordered INCR files carry later writes and HISTORY files become cleanup candidates. The configuration explicitly exposes a speed/data-safety choice; it is not proof that any deployment uses that default.

## Architecture trace

During multi-part AOF rewriting, a new base and ongoing increments are coordinated through manifest state rather than treated as one overwritten file. The selected aof.c comments define which files remain authoritative; the configuration and live documentation explain when disk synchronization is requested and how a rewrite-related option can weaken that policy. Source/configuration inspection did not observe a write acknowledgment, fsync completion, restart or recovery.

## What to borrow and adapt

Ask what loss window the product can tolerate and identify which acknowledged operations may not yet have crossed a durable boundary. Model rewrite/compaction as a lifecycle with old and new authoritative sets, not a background operation assumed to be harmless. Keep backup/recovery verification separate from persistence and from replication.

## Diagram implications

Show memory, base snapshot, incremental log files, manifest and disk synchronization as separate concepts. Annotate the selected policy and rewrite handoff. A replication arrow would not by itself demonstrate disk durability. A sequence or state view can expose interruption between producing a new base and publishing its manifest.

## Mismatches and limits

Public documentation includes broad durability shorthand; this card does not treat it as a universal data-loss upper bound across storage, OS and configuration failures. The inspected source is a pinned development snapshot and the docs are mutable. No current cluster configuration, replication guarantee, fault injection, backup restoration or performance comparison was tested.

# Boundaries, state and failure reasoning

Use this when evaluating responsibility boundaries, coordination, persistent state or migration. Follow one operation end to end before multiplying components.

## Make boundaries meaningful

Name what each boundary owns: a change-prone decision, public contract, state transition, transaction, deployment, trust relationship or operational responsibility. Different boundary kinds answer different questions. Draw the one needed for the decision and label it; physical folders or service nouns alone are insufficient.

Identify who can authoritatively change each important state. A derived index, cache or read model needs an update/rebuild path and a staleness policy. Separate the authoritative write from projections and notifications. A shared database can provide useful local transactions while coupling schema ownership; separate databases do not create independent business invariants automatically.

Trace a concrete input through validation, coordination, state mutation, external effect and response. Note where control returns, durability is assumed and failure can leave an uncertain result. Check the actual implementation/configuration contract rather than inferring guarantees from an API name or architecture diagram.

## Treat coordination claims precisely

For asynchronous work, distinguish:

- Request accepted from durable state committed.
- Event/message persisted from delivered or processed.
- Handler returned from external side effect confirmed.
- Acknowledgment from the underlying business operation's outcome.

Repeated delivery can be harmless under an operation-specific idempotency contract; a delivery mechanism's deduplication window is not necessarily that contract. A local inbox/outbox transaction does not automatically include an external provider. A timeout can mean unknown result, not proof of failure. Reconciliation may be needed before another external attempt; inventing a refund/cancellation API does not make an irreversible effect reversible.

Specify which consistency property matters to which operation under which failure model. Linearizable observation, transactional atomicity, replica convergence, availability, latency and durability are distinct. “CAP chooses two” or “eventual consistency” is too vague to decide single-use redemption, stale browsing, inventory reservation or offline edits. State exact assumptions before applying a theorem or a product claim.

Queueing, retries and caches can move or amplify load. Identify admission/rate limits, bounded capacity, retry/backoff policy and the observed signal for overload if relevant. Do not claim unbounded retry fixes reliability or a new queue creates throughput. Report workload assumptions and what measurement would discriminate alternatives.

## Evolve without skipping the transition

Map current/proposed/intermediate states. Identify authoritative data during migration, compatibility between old/new producers and consumers, cutover conditions and what can be rolled back. Dual writes, backfills, shadow reads and replay each have failure and reconciliation assumptions; they are not automatically safer than a smaller in-place change.

Preserve public behavior and operator capacity when requested. A strangler boundary may isolate a change, but does not settle state ownership or guarantee zero downtime. A new dependency/service requires a contextual benefit, owner and failure plan. An assessment can stop at the evidence needed to choose that transition; it does not authorize executing it.

Use exact [system cases and pattern cards](../library/index.md) for specific mechanisms, including explicit mismatches and source versions. Do not import a distributed platform's entire operating model into a small tool because one coordination idea is useful.

# Context, consequential questions and architectural tradeoffs

Use this when a design request lacks its operating conditions or when multiple plausible architectures solve different problems. Do not turn the table into a mandatory questionnaire.

| Decision input | Inspect first | Ask only what remains consequential |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Behavior and invariant | Contracts, operation paths, known incidents and data ownership | What outcome must never happen, and what degraded result is acceptable? |
| Workload | Available measurements, data sizes, concurrency and growth records | Which scenario matters and what growth/latency assumptions should guide a proposal? |
| Deployment and operations | Current configuration/topology, permitted dependencies, ownership | Who will operate added components and what operating cost can the team sustain? |
| State and compatibility | Authoritative stores, transaction boundaries, consumers, API/event versions | Which stale/duplicate/partial observations are acceptable, and what must remain compatible? |
| Evolution | Actual change pressure, migration options and constraints | Which capability must change independently, and how much transition risk is acceptable? |

Separate a business rule from its current implementation. A user can know the cost of duplicate fulfillment without choosing a queue technology. A source tree can reveal current calls but not whether a latency target is negotiable. Do not ask people to invent an answer to a discoverable technical fact.

Make quality requirements operational: a named stimulus, environment, affected operation/state, required response and measure if supplied. “Reliable,” “scalable” and “clean” alone do not select a design. If measurements or a policy are absent, use an explicit conditional recommendation or a labeled provisional model; do not add precise invented targets.

## Compare under the same constraints

For each serious option, identify the invariant it can enforce, state/coordination ownership, normal/failure path, operational burden, compatibility/migration cost and unresolved evidence. Retain meaningful alternatives without building every one. Existing in-process boundaries or a single deployment are valid candidates. Distribution can support independent deployment or fault/resource isolation while adding partial failures, consistency and operations work.

A directory/module can hide a change-prone decision without being a service. A semantic/domain boundary can be useful without a process boundary. Conversely, a single deployment does not guarantee that internal modules remain independent. Compare actual interfaces and coordination needs rather than declaring either form inherently superior.

Read original arguments with their stated uncertainty. A conceptual design argument, a formal impossibility proof, an author's system report and a controlled experiment support different claims. Preserve disagreement about assumptions instead of selecting whichever slogan supports a preferred pattern. Use the [library](../library/index.md) to find the relevant primary portions and contrasting cases.

## Compact decision record

A useful record can be a few paragraphs: context/decision question, chosen mechanism, alternatives and decisive reason, consequences/assumptions, status and evidence that would reopen it. Keep accepted, proposed, superseded and historical decisions distinguishable. A decision record is not proof the design was deployed or remains current.

When feedback arrives, revise the affected choice and corresponding diagrams. If an unknown-field policy, offline requirement or operating budget invalidates a provisional architecture, retire that branch rather than asking the person to choose between obsolete technology options. A full brief or explicit delegation does not need another style vote.
